content: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a condition where sustained aerobic exercise leads to shortness of breath due to acute narrowing of the airways. This condition is particularly common in individuals with bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Unlike other forms of asthma, EIA does not appear to be caused by the same inflammatory mechanisms, although it shares many clinical features and responds to some of the same medications. Pathogenesis The exact mechanisms underlying EIA are not fully understood. Typically, EIA occurs after several minutes of vigorous aerobic activity. During exercise, individuals often switch from nasal breathing to mouth breathing, which results in the inhalation of air that is not adequately warmed or humidified. This leads to increased blood flow to the bronchial lining, causing edema and subsequent constriction of the bronchial vessels. This process results in airflow obstruction and symptoms similar to other forms of asthma, but without the inflammatory changes seen in those conditions. Epidemiology and Demographics EIA affects approximately 7-20% of the general population. Among individuals with asthma, the majority experience some degree of exercise-induced symptoms. Diagnosis History and Symptoms EIA typically begins with an initial phase of bronchodilation occurring 6-8 minutes after exercise, followed by bronchospasm. Symptoms usually resolve completely within an hour. If exercise is resumed during this period, symptoms are often mild or absent. A refractory period often follows the resolution of an attack, likely due to the release of inhibitory prostaglandins such as prostaglandin E2. Approximately 6-10 hours after an initial attack, a rebound episode with milder symptoms may occur, even without further exertion. Severe attacks are more likely in individuals with both allergic and exercise-induced asthma, particularly when exercising in high-allergen environments (e.g., walking uphill near slow-moving traffic at dusk). Such attacks can be life-threatening. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, and, in severe cases, altered mental status due to hypoxia. Physical Examination Vital Signs Tachypnea (rapid breathing) Tachycardia (elevated heart rate) HEENT (Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat) Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin) may occur in severe cases due to hypoxia. Lungs A high-pitched, prolonged expiratory wheeze may be audible, even without a stethoscope. Other Diagnostic Studies Exercise Challenge Test The exercise challenge test is a direct diagnostic method. A positive test is indicated by a 10% reduction in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second) after 6-8 minutes of treadmill exercise. In athletes, this test can confirm airway narrowing due to exercise and guide treatment with inhaled corticosteroids, which often reduce respiratory symptoms during exercise. For example, some athletes utilize the refractory period by warming up to induce a mild attack and timing their competition during the refractory phase. Stepwise training with increasing intensity can achieve a similar effect. Therapy should be monitored regularly, with peak expiratory flow rate assessments performed before and after exercise. The methacholine challenge test is another option to evaluate treatment response objectively. Fish oil supplementation may offer non-pharmacologic benefits for individuals with EIA. Pharmacological Interventions Beta-agonists, such as salmeterol, formoterol, and terbutaline, are commonly used 20 minutes before exercise to prevent symptoms. These bronchodilators are effective in the short term but may lose efficacy with repeated use (tachyphylaxis). However, they remain highly effective when used immediately before exercise. Cromolyn and nedocromil, administered via aerosol, provide protection against EIA in children. Combining cromolyn with beta-agonists may offer additional benefits, particularly for high-performance athletes. Inhaled corticosteroids, when used for weeks or months before exercise, significantly reduce exercise-induced bronchoconstriction but do not provide immediate relief. Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, has shown significant protective effects against EIA and reduces urinary leukotriene excretion after exercise. However, leukotriene inhibitors are not effective in all patients. Other potential pharmacological agents include frusemide, prostaglandin E2, indomethacin, and heparin. Prognosis The prognosis for individuals with EIA is generally excellent, as evidenced by numerous professional athletes who have successfully managed the condition. Notable examples include Olympic swimmers Tom Dolan, Amy Van Dyken, and Nancy Hogshead, baseball Hall of Famer Catfish Hunter, and football player Jerome Bettis. However, it is worth noting that a significant proportion of Olympic athletes report having asthma, which some experts attribute to the potential performance-enhancing effects of asthma medications. Future or Investigational Therapies A randomized crossover study comparing oral montelukast with inhaled salmeterol found both drugs to be similarly effective, though montelukast provided benefits lasting up to 24 hours. In a large randomized study involving children, montelukast monotherapy and combination therapy with montelukast and budesonide were more effective than budesonide monotherapy or combined therapy with budesonide and formoterol.
